myth: A lump in the breast always means cancer.
why_people_believe: People hear stories of lumps that turned out to be cancer.
fact: Many lumps are not cancer. Only a health worker can check. Still, every new lump should be examined.
what_to_do: See a clinic if you find a new lump. Do not wait at home in fear.

myth: Breast cancer is a curse or punishment.
why_people_believe: Illness is sometimes explained through spiritual blame.
fact: Breast cancer is a disease of cells. It is not a curse. Treatment and support exist.
what_to_do: Seek medical care and kind support. You are not to blame.

myth: Only women who have many partners get cervical cancer.
why_people_believe: People link the cervix only to sexual behaviour.
fact: HPV is common. Most sexually active people meet it. Screening and vaccines protect everyone who needs them.
what_to_do: Get screened when invited. Ask about the HPV vaccine for young people in your family.

myth: If I feel well, I do not need a cervical screening.
why_people_believe: People wait for pain before they visit a clinic.
fact: Early cervical changes often have no pain. Screening finds them before they become cancer.
what_to_do: Go for screening even if you feel fine. Ask a nurse when you are due.

myth: Prostate problems are just old age and cannot be treated.
why_people_believe: Urine changes are common in older men, so people ignore them.
fact: Some urine changes are not cancer, but some are. A health worker can check and treat many problems.
what_to_do: Tell a clinic if passing urine becomes hard, painful, or bloody.

myth: Talking about the prostate is shameful for men.
why_people_believe: Men are often told to stay silent about the body.
fact: Silence delays care. Prostate cancer found early is often treatable.
what_to_do: Talk to a trusted health worker. Bring a friend if that feels easier.

myth: Yellow eyes always mean witchcraft.
why_people_believe: Jaundice looks sudden and frightening.
fact: Yellow skin or eyes can be a liver problem, including hepatitis or cancer. It needs a clinic, not blame.
what_to_do: Go to a health facility the same week you notice yellow eyes or skin.

myth: Hepatitis vaccines are only for babies and do not matter.
why_people_believe: Adults think vaccines stop after childhood.
fact: Hepatitis B vaccine lowers the chance of liver cancer. Ask if you still need it.
what_to_do: Ask a clinic about hepatitis B vaccination and testing.

myth: Blood in the stool is always haemorrhoids.
why_people_believe: Haemorrhoids are common, so people self-diagnose.
fact: Blood in the stool can have many causes. A health worker should check, especially if it is new or lasts.
what_to_do: Do not treat yourself for weeks. Book a clinic visit.

myth: Only rich countries get bowel cancer.
why_people_believe: People think this cancer is a Western disease.
fact: Colorectal cancer occurs in Africa too. Diet, family history, and age all matter.
what_to_do: Tell a health worker about lasting bowel changes. Ask about screening if you are 50 or older.

myth: Only grown-ups get lumps in the chest.
why_people_believe: Kids think illness is only for older people.
fact: Anyone can find a new lump. Most lumps are not cancer, but a grown-up should still tell a nurse.
what_to_do: If you feel a new lump, tell a parent or teacher. Ask to see a health worker.

myth: You do not need to check your body until you are old.
why_people_believe: Teens think breast checks are only for older women.
fact: Knowing what is normal for your body helps you notice a change early. A health worker can teach you.
what_to_do: Learn how your chest usually feels. Tell a clinic if you find a new lump or a change.

myth: Shots are only for when you already feel sick.
why_people_believe: Kids think medicine is only for pain.
fact: Some shots, like the HPV vaccine when you are older, help stop illness before it starts.
what_to_do: Ask a parent about vaccines at the clinic. They keep your body safer.

myth: The HPV vaccine is only for girls who have had sex.
why_people_believe: People mix up HPV with blame about sex.
fact: HPV is common. The vaccine works best before exposure. Boys and girls can both be protected when it is offered.
what_to_do: Ask a clinic or a trusted adult about the HPV vaccine. It is a health choice, not a judgement.

myth: Boys should never talk about how they pee.
why_people_believe: Kids are told that body talk is rude.
fact: Peeing is a normal body job. Pain or blood is a reason to tell a grown-up, not a secret.
what_to_do: If peeing hurts or looks odd, tell a parent and see a nurse.

myth: Young men never need to notice changes when they urinate.
why_people_believe: People say prostate care is only for old men.
fact: Prostate cancer is more common later in life, but urine pain or blood at any age should be checked.
what_to_do: Do not stay quiet. Tell a health worker if passing urine becomes hard, painful, or bloody.

myth: Only grown-ups get sick from smoking.
why_people_believe: Kids see adults smoke and think the harm is far away.
fact: Smoke is not safe for anyone. It can hurt the lungs and the liver over time.
what_to_do: Stay away from smoke. Tell a grown-up if someone offers you a cigarette.

myth: Smoking and alcohol cannot hurt you until you are old.
why_people_believe: Teens think damage only shows after many years.
fact: Smoke and heavy alcohol can harm the liver. Hepatitis vaccines also help protect the liver.
what_to_do: Skip smoking. Limit alcohol. Ask a clinic about hepatitis B vaccination.

myth: Tummy pain is always from snacks, so you can ignore it.
why_people_believe: Kids get tummy aches often and wait for them to pass.
fact: A tummy ache that lasts, or blood in the toilet, needs a grown-up and a nurse.
what_to_do: Tell a parent if your tummy hurts for many days or if you see blood.

myth: Checking your body is embarrassing, so skip it.
why_people_believe: Teens feel shy about toilets and blood.
fact: Blood in the stool or a lasting change in the toilet is a reason to see a health worker, not to hide.
what_to_do: Tell a trusted adult or a clinic. Early checks are kinder than waiting in fear.

myth: Cancer is always an immediate death sentence and cannot be cured or treated.
why_people_believe: People often meet cancer late, when treatment is harder.
fact: Caught early, cervical, breast, and prostate cancers can often be treated. Many people in East Africa live after care.
what_to_do: Learn the signs, get screened, and see a health worker early.
